title: Client-Side Data Fetching
description: Learn when and how to fetch data on the client using useEffect, the React use() hook, and modern patterns for interactive Next.js applications.

data.text: Server Components handle most data fetching in Next.js, but some scenarios require fetching data on the client. When a component needs to respond to user input, browser events, or real-time updates, you need a Client Component that runs in the browser.
Client-side data fetching means requesting data after the page has already loaded. The browser downloads the page first, then the JavaScript runs and fetches additional data as needed.
When to Fetch on the Client

items: The data depends on user input, like search queries or form fields
You need real-time updates from WebSockets or polling
The component uses browser-only APIs like localStorage or geolocation
The data updates frequently and does not need server-side caching

data.text: The most common pattern is using the useEffect hook with useState to manage loading and error states. You start with an empty state, trigger the fetch in useEffect, and update the state when the response arrives.

data.title: Fetching with useState and useEffect
data.content: Fetching data on the client with useState, useEffect, and an abort-like cleanup pattern.

data.text: React also provides a use() hook that lets you read promises and context directly in render. Next.js extends this so you can use it in Server Components alongside Suspense boundaries for streaming. On the client, use() unwraps a promise and triggers the closest Suspense boundary while waiting.

data.title: Using the use() hook in a Client Component
data.content: Using React's use() hook to unwrap a promise inside a Client Component.

data.title: Watch Out
data.text: Client Components increase the JavaScript sent to the browser. Always ask whether the data could be fetched in a Server Component before moving logic to the client.

When a component unmounts before a fetch completes, the state update can cause a memory leak. Use a cleanup flag inside useEffect to ignore stale responses. For AbortController, call abort() in the cleanup function to cancel the in-flight request.

data.title: Aborting in-flight requests on unmount
data.content: Using AbortController to cancel in-flight requests when the component unmounts or query changes.

data.title: Summary
points: Use client-side data fetching when the data depends on browser state or user input.
The useEffect hook with useState remains the standard pattern for client fetches.
React's use() hook offers a cleaner alternative when combined with Suspense.
Always clean up requests to prevent memory leaks and state updates on unmounted components.
